procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 15.11.2018 of the High Court of Madhya Pradesh at Indore in CRRFC No.04 of 2018 and CRA No. 4379 of 2018.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Trial Court awarded a death sentence to the appellant. The appellant preferred an appeal (CRA No. 4379 of 2018) to the High Court of Madhya Pradesh, Bench at Indore, challenging his conviction and sentence. The Trial Court also forwarded a death reference (CRRFC No. 04 of 2018) to the High Court for confirmation of the death sentence. The High Court dismissed the appellant's appeal and affirmed the death sentence.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant approached the Supreme Court by way of Criminal Appeals Nos. 572-573 of 2019, assailing the correctness of the High Court's judgment and order which affirmed the death sentence awarded by the Trial Court and dismissed the appellant's appeal.

issue.issue_text: Whether the conviction of an accused is required to be set aside upon a finding that they were a juvenile at the time of the commission of the offence.

facts: An accused person was convicted by a regular criminal court (Sessions Court).
During the appeal process, the accused raised a claim of juvenility for the first time, asserting they were a child at the time the offense was committed.
An inquiry confirmed that the accused was indeed a juvenile on the date of the offense.
law: Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection) Act, 2015, Section 9(3): This section allows a claim of juvenility to be raised at any stage.

Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2000, Section 7A: This provision states that upon a finding of juvenility, the court must forward the juvenile to the Juvenile Justice Board (JJB) for appropriate orders, and any sentence passed by the regular court shall be deemed to have no effect.
Legal Maxim - *expression unius est exclusion alterius*: This principle of statutory interpretation means that the express mention of one thing implies the exclusion of another.
application: The Supreme Court analyzed the text of the Juvenile Justice Acts and found no provision that requires a conviction to be set aside upon a finding of juvenility.
The Court noted that the law explicitly states that the *sentence* passed by a regular court shall have no effect, and the matter must be sent to the Juvenile Justice Board for appropriate orders.

Applying the maxim *expression unius est exclusion alterius*, the Court reasoned that because the legislature specifically mandated setting aside the sentence but was silent about the conviction, it did not intend for the conviction to be overturned.

The Court concluded that the legislative intent was to grant the benefits of the juvenile justice system to the accused at the sentencing stage, not to invalidate the entire trial or the finding of guilt (the conviction).

The Court also reviewed past judgments and found that while some had set aside convictions, they did so without laying down a clear legal principle or ratio on the issue, thus not creating a binding precedent.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that a conviction recorded by a Sessions Court is not vitiated or required to be set aside merely because the accused is later found to have been a juvenile at the time of the offense. The trial and the finding of guilt remain valid; only the sentence is affected and must be determined by the Juvenile Justice Board in accordance with juvenile law.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the conviction of an accused is required to be set aside upon a finding that they were a juvenile at the time of the commission of the offence.
appellant_arguments: The appellant's conviction and sentence should be set aside because they were a juvenile at the time the offence was committed.
respondent_arguments: The conviction should not be set aside, even if the accused is found to have been a juvenile at the time of the offence.

cases.principle: When an accused is found to be a juvenile on the date of the offence, the court should set aside the sentence of imprisonment awarded but not the conviction itself.

cases.case_name: Ashok Kumar Mehra and Another vs. State of Punjab and Others
cases.principle: When an accused is found to be a juvenile on the date of the offence, the court should set aside the sentence of imprisonment awarded but not the conviction itself.

cases.case_name: Jitendra Singh alias Babboo Singh and another vs. State of Uttar Pradesh
cases.principle: When an accused is found to be a juvenile on the date of the offence, the court should set aside the sentence of imprisonment awarded but not the conviction itself.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When a claim of juvenility is established after a conviction by a regular criminal court, the law does not require the conviction to be set aside; it only requires the sentence of imprisonment to be quashed.
obiter: Applying the maxim expression unius est exclusion alterius, it would be reasonable to hold that the law insofar as it requires a reference to be made to the Board excludes by necessary implication any intention on the part of the legislature requiring the courts to set aside the conviction recorded by the lower court.

Parliament, it appears, was content with setting aside the sentence of imprisonment awarded to the juvenile and making of a reference to the Board without specifically or by implication requiring the court concerned to alter or set aside the conviction.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: A finding that an accused was a juvenile at the time of the offence does not require the conviction itself to be set aside. The court's reasoning distinguishes between the finding of guilt and the imposition of sentence. Based on established legal precedent, the court affirmed the conviction on its merits, finding no reason to interfere with the conclusions of the lower courts, while simultaneously setting aside the sentence as it could not have been imposed on a juvenile.
legal_tests_applied: The court's reasoning is based on adherence to precedent, explicitly stating: "we approve the view taken by this court in the case of Jitendra Singh (supra), Mahesh (supra) and Satya Deo (supra)."
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument to set aside the conviction failed because the court, after reviewing the record, found "no ground whatsoever to take a view different from what has been recorded by the learned trial Court and affirmed by the High Court" regarding the finding of guilt.

The legal position, as affirmed by the court through prior judgments, is that a conviction is not nullified simply because the offender is subsequently found to have been a juvenile at the time of the crime.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's argument to uphold the conviction succeeded because the court found no reason to interfere with the merits of the conviction, stating that it "shall stand affirmed."

The court's decision was based on the established legal principle, drawn from the cases of Jitendra Singh, Mahesh, and Satya Deo, that a finding of juvenility affects the sentence but does not automatically vitiate the conviction itself.
